name: Colchagua Valley
shape: Chile Decreto 464, drawn from its comunas and provinces

climate: Seasons this mild ripen Chardonnay, Riesling, Pinot Noir, Sauvignon Blanc and Sémillon fully without cooking off their freshness.
Chardonnay sits in its sweet spot, so the wines can show the style it is known for.
Cabernet Sauvignon is at its cool limit. In cool years it can stay underripe, with green, sharp flavors.
Merlot is at its cool limit. In cool years it can stay underripe, with green, sharp flavors.
Syrah is at its cool limit. In cool years it can stay underripe, with green, sharp flavors.
Most rain falls in winter. Dry summers keep mildew and rot down, though young vines may need watering.

soil.rock: Granite weathers to coarse, acid, free-draining soil that warms quickly and holds heat. Its acidity tends to lower the grapes' acidity, which suits Gamay. Volcanic rock is porous, so it drains well and sends roots deep. Lava soils are mostly basalt, rich in iron, calcium and magnesium.
soil.top: The topsoil holds water well and drains at a steady pace, so vines rarely go thirsty or sit in wet ground. Its pH is close to neutral, so vines take up the nutrients they need easily.

land: The high ground runs about 4°F cooler than the low ground. Higher vineyards ripen later and keep more acidity, so one grape can make lighter or richer wine here depending on height.
Much of it is steep. Cold air and rain run off, so frost and waterlogging are rare and soils stay thin, keeping yields low. Steep rows are slow and costly to work, often by hand.
